source_text: Credit quippe adversum nos Manichaeus naturaliter mortales in flagitia facinoraque compelli; opinatur tenebrarum originem et corporibus materiam et criminibus praestitisse; voluptatem sexuum tabem esse generis humani, assertricem iuris diabolici, et in universa dedecora hominum coactricem. Quem Traducianus omnifariam secutus, quippe eius haeres et soboles, naturalia crimina, aeternam de tenebroso nihilo mali necessitatem, et affectionem sensibus destinatam sanctorum omnium pollutricem atque imaginem Dei in regno diaboli collocantem, oratione multiplici testatur.
pass_a_gloss: For Manichaeus believes against us that mortals are naturally compelled into outrages and crimes; he opines that an origin of darkness furnished both matter for bodies and for charges; that the pleasure of the sexes is a wasting of the human race, an asserter of diabolical right, and a co-forcer of humans into all dishonors. Whom the Traducian having followed in every way, seeing that he is his heir and offspring, testifies by a multiple speech natural charges, an eternal necessity of evil from a dark nothing, and an affection destined for the senses as a polluter of all the holy and as placing the image of God in the devil's kingdom.

lemmas.lexica: Julian's polemic label for teachers of tradux peccati
LS tradux=vine-shoot/layer; Blaise tradux peccati=transmission of sin by descent
LS necessitas; Blaise vs free choice
Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: Against us, Mani believes mortals are driven by nature into shameful acts and crimes. He supposes the origin of darkness supplied the material both for bodies and for crimes; that sexual pleasure is the corruption of the human race, the vindication of the devil’s claim, and the force driving people into every dishonor. The advocate of inherited sin follows him in every way, as his heir and offspring, repeatedly proclaiming natural crimes, an eternal necessity of evil arising from dark nothingness, and an affection assigned to the senses that pollutes all the saints and places God’s image in the devil’s kingdom.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
